subtype: Approach: test skills without the tool to catch dependence [Revision]
passage:
Pranav stared at the blank page on the verandah step, the cooling tea beside him. His seminar paragraph was due, and without the tool open he could not get past two clumsy lines. It scared him a little: when had that happened?

He told his friend Raghav, who lived in the next lane. Raghav shrugged and said, "Then measure it." They made a plan. Every evening after dinner, one tool-free hour of writing, then, each Sunday, a paragraph on a fresh topic in twenty minutes, with Raghav marking it for clarity out of five.

The first Sunday he scored two. By the fourth, he scored four, and the phrases had begun to come back without prompting.

qa.q: How long was the Sunday paragraph test?
qa.a: Twenty minutes, on a fresh topic.

qa.q: What did Pranav feel when he could not get past two clumsy lines?
qa.a: Pranav felt scared and a little shaken, wondering when he had lost the ability to write on his own.

qa.q: What could Pranav do beside the weekly test to keep improving, and why?
qa.a: Pranav could read good writing and copy out sentences by hand, because noticing how others build sentences trains his own without the tool.

qa.q: How might Raghav see marking Pranav's paragraphs each Sunday?
qa.a: Raghav probably feels like a useful ally, seeing Pranav's score climb from two to four and knowing the blunt remark started it.

grounding: After finding it hard to write unaided, the person schedules tool-free practice and a weekly self-test, revealing overreliance early.

subtype: Approach: test skills without the tool to catch dependence [Revision]

The exam hall in Aarhus had no laptops allowed, only paper and a clock. The question asked Emil to argue for or against free public transport in one clear paragraph. Forty minutes later, Emil had four crossed-out sentences and a headache. For a year every paragraph had started with a prompt to a chatbot, and without it the ideas just sat there, loose.
That evening Emil told Astrid, his flatmate, "I think I can't write any more. Not really."
"So practise without it," she said, "and check."
He took a calendar and blocked two slots: Tuesday and Thursday, forty-five minutes, laptop in the drawer, pen only. Every Sunday he pulled a random topic from a jar Astrid filled and gave himself twenty minutes to write one paragraph, then timed and saved it.
By the third Sunday the paragraph came out whole, rough but his.

qa.q: How long did Emil give himself for the Sunday paragraph?
qa.a: He gave himself twenty minutes to write one paragraph.

qa.q: How did Emil feel after the exam, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt shaken and a bit ashamed, telling Astrid 'I think I can't write any more' after forty minutes of crossed-out sentences.

qa.q: What else could Emil do to catch dependence early in other skills?
qa.a: He could run the same kind of short, tool-free test for reading summaries or problem solving, so any weak spot shows up before an exam does.

qa.q: How might Astrid see the change over three weeks?
qa.a: Astrid, who filled the topic jar, sees a flatmate who went from panic to producing rough but whole paragraphs, and may feel quietly proud to have helped.

grounding: Shows the person noticing it is hard to write unaided, then planning tool-free practice and a weekly timed test to measure the skill.

The placement cell's written round had one section Tarun hadn't expected: draft a polite email to a client about a delayed shipment, by hand, in fifteen minutes. He stared at the sheet. He usually typed three words into a chatbot and polished what came back. Now he wrote "Dear Sir" and stopped.
Afterwards, Rekha, the placement officer, went through the scripts with the students. "Yours is half a page of beginnings," she said kindly.
Tarun went quiet on the walk back to the hostel. That night he made a plan on a sheet taped above his desk: Monday, Wednesday, Friday, one email or paragraph by hand, no tool. Saturday, a self-test: a prompt from a list of old placement questions, fifteen minutes, then compare with a model answer.
Two weeks later his Saturday email filled the page, with a clear apology and a new date.

qa.q: How long did the placement round give for the email?
qa.a: It gave fifteen minutes to write the email by hand.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling on the walk back to the hostel?
qa.a: He was likely embarrassed and worried, going quiet after realising he could barely start an email without the tool.

qa.q: What other approach could help Tarun, and why?
qa.a: He could ask Rekha for feedback on one practice email each week, since an outside eye would show gaps he might not notice alone.

qa.q: How might Rekha see Tarun's change?
qa.a: Rekha, who told him kindly about his half page of beginnings, would likely be encouraged to see a full, clear email two weeks later.

grounding: Shows the person discovering dependence in a written test, then scheduling tool-free practice and a weekly self-test to track the skill.
